mirror.title: Technique: The Self-Criticism Mirror
mirror.description: This practice helps you see just how harsh your inner critic can be. Through a brief role-play, you’ll direct your usual self-critical phrases toward a loved one to feel how they sound from an outside perspective. This exercise helps you notice the unfairness of self-criticism and encourages a kinder attitude toward yourself.

texts: <activitylink id="alkjnaNNasz">
Try this: imagine holding a loved one to the same harsh standards you usually hold yourself to. Be honest with yourself as you do it.
Very often, within the first few minutes, it becomes clear just how harsh and unfair inner criticism can be.
Let’s look at this exercise through an example of a dialogue between a client and a psychologist:
<dialog psy="true">Dmitry, you mentioned that losing your job made you feel like a failure, leading to thoughts like, “I’m a loser, I can’t do anything right.”</dialog>

<dialog psy="true">Let’s look at these thoughts from a different angle. I suggest we try a mini role-play: you’ll say your critical phrases, but instead of directing them at yourself, you’ll address them to a loved one—for example, your best friend.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">I’ll play the role of a friend who also lost their job. You play yourself. Ready to try?</dialog>
<dialog man="true">Yes, let’s try.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">Let’s begin. I’ll say: “I was let go from my job today.”</dialog>
<dialog man="true">Maybe… you did something wrong. Otherwise, they wouldn’t have let you go.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">What exactly, do you think?</dialog>
<dialog man="true">Well… maybe you made a mistake, or you weren’t attentive enough.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">So, you’re criticizing me right now?</dialog>
<dialog man="true">I suppose so. It seems like you weren’t handling it well. Maybe you’re just not good enough at your job.</dialog>
<dialog psy="true">That’s very painful to hear. I was hoping for support.</dialog>
<dialog man="true">I understand… but if you made mistakes and couldn’t handle it, how can I support you?</dialog>

After this role-play, Dmitry said it was incredibly difficult to say those things to someone close to him. He realized that in real life, he would never treat someone that way—yet he did it to himself constantly.
<q author="Brené Brown">Talk to yourself the way you would talk to someone you love.</q>
Interesting, isn’t it? Things we find almost impossible to say to others, we sometimes say to ourselves quite easily.
We often show patience, gentleness, and understanding to others—and completely forget to show them to ourselves.
Try to let go of double standards. You also deserve respect, support, and kindness.
Remember: healthy self-esteem is a key foundation for your motivation, goals, and life energy.
When self-esteem is low, we underestimate our abilities, almost as if we are denying ourselves the right to be happy.
Start gradually changing how you treat yourself: acknowledge small wins, allow yourself to be human, to make mistakes, and to learn. Small steps lead to big changes.

mistake.title: Technique: Overcoming the Fear of Making Mistakes
mistake.description: This article offers effective methods to combat perfectionism, helping you embrace imperfection and reduce the fear of making mistakes.

texts: Let’s look at a few simple yet highly effective methods to help you overcome the urge toward perfectionism.
The “anti-perfectionism” log
<activitylink id="naslSLnadfl">
Many perfectionists live with the belief that they can only fully enjoy something if it is performed perfectly. We invite you to challenge this idea.
For one week, keep a log of various spontaneous tasks you complete, whether it’s “brushing your teeth,” “making dinner,” “preparing a work report,” or “cleaning the house.”
In the second column, note how effectively you believe the task was completed, expressed as a percentage.
In the third column, note how much joy completing it brought you.
Examples might look like this:
• Making dinner – 50% (could have chosen a more complex and tasty recipe) – 90% (simple, but so delicious and didn’t take much time).
• Cleaning the house – 70% (did all the main things, but didn’t get to the fridge or the stove) – 100% (a clean house always brings me joy).
• Preparing a work report – 85% (put a lot of effort into the report) – 20% (constant thoughts about how it could have been better robbed me of the joy of the process).
This exercise will help you realize that achieving perfection is not a prerequisite for enjoying the process.
<q author="Thomas Watson">Perfection is not an attainable goal, but a direction to move in.</q>
Embracing the possibility of making mistakes
<activitylink id="lsvnnDSnsdl">
Nobody likes making mistakes, but for perfectionists, they can become a source of intense fear.
One of the most effective ways to overcome the fear of imperfection is to learn to accept your mistakes.
Do you feel your heart race at the mere thought of a possible mistake? These are signs of fear and anxiety.
To become more open to the possibility of making mistakes, start by writing an essay on why mistakes are normal and why striving for absolute perfection is irrational.
One young woman struggling with perfectionism shared these thoughts:

<dialog>The fear of making a mistake comes from my black-and-white thinking: one mistake, and everything collapses. This is a misconception. A small mistake cannot destroy all the good that has been done.</dialog>

<dialog>Mistakes are useful because they allow us to learn. Without mistakes, learning is impossible. Since no one is immune to making mistakes, it is important to learn to accept them and continue learning from our own experiences.</dialog>
<dialog>Acknowledging mistakes allows us to adjust our behavior, which leads to more satisfying results, making us happier and improving our quality of life.</dialog>
<dialog>Most people won’t judge us for our mistakes or stop loving us because of them—after all, everyone makes mistakes, and many feel uncomfortable in a society of “perfect” people.</dialog>
<dialog>A mistake is not the end of the world.</dialog>
Of course, creating such a list doesn’t mean an instant transformation or an immediate love for mistakes, but it is an important step toward changing your attitude toward imperfection.

Write your own essay on why it is normal and even helpful to make mistakes. Remind yourself that even if you make a mistake, the world won’t end—it is a natural part of any process, even if it isn’t the most pleasant one.

nonDepression.title: Being sad doesn’t mean you have depression
nonDepression.description: In this article, we discuss the important distinction between natural sadness and clinical depression. Loss, breakups, hardships, and changes are part of life, and it is perfectly human to experience pain. We explain how to distinguish natural emotions from depression, where cognitive distortions play a major role and professional help may be needed. This material will help you better understand your feelings and notice when sadness goes beyond the norm.

texts: In previous sections, we talked about how real and painful events like loss, illness, breakups, betrayal, or job loss can be.
<q author="Viktor Frankl">Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our freedom to choose how we respond. In our response lies our growth and our strength.</q>
Everyone faces similar experiences at some point. They are heavy, deep, and very human. But they do not, in themselves, mean depression.
This raises the question: does “healthy sadness” exist—the kind that isn’t linked to depression?
Of course it does.

<important>Feeling sadness, grief, or longing are natural reactions to significant events, losses, and changes. These feelings help you process experiences, acknowledge what is happening, and move forward.</important>
These are normal human emotions, and it is important to allow yourself to experience them rather than suppressing them or feeling ashamed.
If you are sad after a breakup, that’s normal. It speaks to your ability to feel and to form attachments.
If it hurts to remember a loved one who has passed, that is a reflection of love, not a sign of weakness.
But depression is not just sadness. It is a state created and maintained by a distorted, hopeless view of yourself, the world, and the future.
In depression, the intensity and duration of negative emotions do not match the situation—they are much stronger, deeper, and heavier.
When someone with depression faces even ordinary difficulties, they can be perceived as a catastrophe.
A small mistake feels like a failure, a setback feels like a tragedy, and grief can feel like endless darkness.
Imagine a faucet with hot and cold water. In everyday life, we switch between emotions—joy, sadness, hope, regret.
<q author="Viktor Frankl">The most beautiful people are those who have gone through pain, loss, and struggle, and yet still found a way upward.</q>

With depression, it’s as if only the “cold tap” is turned on—sadness, anxiety, and hopelessness. This is often not a consequence of the situation itself, but the result of a distorted perception that requires attention and adjustment.
<important>Our attitude toward events plays a huge role. Sadness itself is not dangerous. It becomes dangerous when thoughts turn it into helplessness and despair.</important>
We sincerely hope this section has helped you better understand the nature of depression and recognize its signs.
Here, you learned about the key symptoms of depression and ways to work through your state using various practices and techniques.
You can always return to these materials, reread them, and practice the exercises. We are already preparing new, helpful tools for you.
